- Over 60 days, the IDF will withdraw from its positions and the Lebanese army will deploy across all border crossings and in southern Lebanon.
- There will be no Israeli buffer zone and residents of south Lebanon can return to their homes.

Prime Minister Netanyahu made a public case for the deal last night, saying it would free up Israel to focus on Iran, give troops time to rest until arms transfers increase under the Trump administration, and isolate Hamas in Gaza, thereby advancing a hostage deal.

Opposition figures were sharply critical, saying the deal would not restore security to the north and sacrificed gains against Hezbollah. Several highlighted the fact that the government signed a deal with Hezbollah before an agreement to free the hostages held by Hamas in Gaza.

Public opinion is generally negative. Flash polling showed only 20% of coalition voters and half of opposition voters supported the deal (37% overall). Half believe the war’s outcome is indecisive and nearly 60% expect the ceasefire to last a few months at most.

While President Biden said the deal is supposed to be a permanent ceasefire, this is unlikely to be the last Israel-Hezbollah clash. Many Israelis do not feel safe enough to return to their homes in the north, and both sides have reasons to be unsatisfied with the outcome.

The deal is an about-face for Hezbollah, which long insisted that any ceasefire had to be linked to one in Gaza. Hamas will now be fighting Israel alone. Yet while this war leaves Hezbollah in a battered state, it remains a serious and strategic threat to Israel.
